original_question: Given k consecutive composite integers n + 1, ..., n + k, must there exist k distinct primes p_1, ..., p_k such that p_j divides n + j for each 1 <= j <= k?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.6 (Grimm) in §1.2, "Exponential Diophantine Equations": given k consecutive composite integers n+1,...,n+k, there exist k distinct primes p_1,...,p_k such that p_j divides n+j for 1≤j≤k. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
correct_elements: Your draft is essentially the paper’s statement verbatim: it has the right objects (k consecutive composite integers n+1,...,n+k), the right conclusion (one prime divisor assigned to each term), and the crucial distinctness requirement on the primes. This matches Conjecture 1.6 exactly, not merely the weaker Conjecture 1.7 about the product having at least k distinct prime divisors. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, quantify explicitly: for every positive integer k and every integer n such that n+1,...,n+k are composite positive integers, does the stated conclusion hold? The paper leaves these quantifiers implicit in the phrase "Given k consecutive composite integers." ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))

Specify that divisibility is in the ring of integers Z and that the p_j are ordinary positive prime numbers. The paper speaks simply of "primes" and "divisible," but a stand-alone version should make the integer setting explicit. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
If desired for paper-faithfulness, identify the problem by name: this is Grimm’s Conjecture. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))

The paper also records an explicitly equivalent reformulation: for increasing positive integers n_1<...<n_k whose product has fewer than k distinct prime factors, there must be a prime in [n_1,n_k]. Including or at least being aware of this equivalence makes the scope sharper. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
refined_question: Is Grimm’s conjecture true? Namely, for every positive integer k and every integer n such that the k consecutive integers n+1,n+2,...,n+k are all composite positive integers, do there exist pairwise distinct primes p_1,p_2,...,p_k with p_j dividing n+j for each j=1,2,...,k? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent formulation stated in the paper: if n_1<...<n_k are increasing positive integers and the product n_1...n_k has fewer than k distinct prime factors, must there exist a prime p with n_1 ≤ p ≤ n_k? The paper says this is equivalent to Grimm’s original formulation, with the equivalence following from the marriage theorem. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))
justification: The draft matches the paper’s Conjecture 1.6 almost word for word, so the nearest official target is exactly Grimm’s Conjecture in §1.2. It should not be replaced by Conjecture 1.7, because the latter is only a weaker statement about the product (n+1)...(n+k) having at least k distinct prime divisors when [n+1,n+k] contains no prime, whereas your draft asks for a distinct prime divisor to be assigned to each individual term n+j. The nearby context in §1.2 places this conjecture among questions on greatest prime factors arising from Baker’s transcendence method, and the paper itself gives the alternate equivalent formulation via the marriage theorem. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0312440))

citations.label: Equivalent rephrasing of Conjecture 1.6 via the marriage theorem
